plot: Odo and Mothwick follow the true story of New England's Dark Day (19 May 1780): the sun vanishes by noon, hens roost, candles are lit and Connecticut's council fears Judgment Day while Abraham Davenport asks for candles; the twist is that tree rings later showed smoke from a distant Canadian forest fire mixed with fog, and the episode ends on huge footprints in the mud.

script.title: 1780: Why Did Noon Turn to Night?

beats.say: It isn't even noon! Why is the sun going out?
A true story. New England, the nineteenth of May, seventeen eighty.
In the middle of the morning, day turned into night. Why?
New episode every day — subscribe so you don't miss what happens next.
A serpent in the harbour, and now the sky goes black?
The water went still, Odo. Now the whole sky has.
In Vermont, the sun was already hidden when it rose that morning.
Thick fog and low cloud hung over the land as well.
In Cambridge, a professor named Samuel Williams watched the sky fade.
Half past ten, and darker still. Note the time exactly.
By noon, people had to light candles just to see indoors.
The hens are going to roost. They think it's night!
In Ipswich, roosters crowed and frogs peeped at two in the afternoon.
Woodcocks whistled their evening calls. In the middle of the day.
What could swallow the sun over a whole country?
The darkness reached from Maine all the way to New Jersey.
And in New Jersey, a young soldier was writing it all down.
The fowls have gone to roost. Whip-poor-wills are singing!
This was seventeen eighty. America was in the middle of a war.
beats.text: IN THE MIDDLE OF A WAR

beats.say: Many people believed it was the end of the world.
In Hartford, Connecticut's leaders were meeting when the darkness came.
This is the Day of Judgment! We must stop and go home!
One man, Abraham Davenport, would not leave his seat.
The day of judgment is either approaching, or it is not.
beats.text: EITHER IT IS, OR IT IS NOT

beats.say: If it is, I choose to be found doing my duty.
I wish, therefore, that candles may be brought.
So they worked by candlelight. The dark lasted deep into the night.
And when the moon finally rose, people said it looked red.
A red moon after a black noon. I don't like this.
Nobody that day could explain it. Not preachers. Not professors.
If the sun can vanish once, Odo, it can vanish again.
The answer waited over two hundred years, hidden inside trees.
Scientists studied old tree rings and fire scars in Ontario, Canada.
They found the marks of a forest fire, burning in seventeen eighty.
Its smoke rolled south, and mixed with that thick fog and cloud.
So the sun was never gone. Just buried in smoke.
Smoke from a fire hundreds of miles away. And nobody knew.
For one day, a whole land lived in the dark.
And one stubborn man asked for candles, and kept on working.
Whatever comes, let it find us doing our duty.
That is the true story of New England's Dark Day.
The sky is clearing, Odo. But look at the mud. Huge footprints.
Next time: a California road crew finds footprints sixteen inches long.
What do you think happens in the next part? Tell me in the comments.

long.title: 1780: Why Did Noon Turn to Night? 🌑 (Ep 49)
long.description:
What do you think happens in the next part? Tell me in the comments.

"Everyone thought the world was ending. One man just asked for candles." — Odo

A true story: on 19 May 1780 the sky over New England went dark by midday. Hens went to roost, candles were lit at noon and the moon rose red. More than 200 years later, tree rings finally gave the answer.

« Tout le monde croyait à la fin du monde. Un homme a simplement demandé des bougies. » — Odo

Une histoire vraie : le 19 mai 1780, le ciel de Nouvelle-Angleterre s'assombrit dès midi. Les poules vont se coucher, on allume des bougies et la lune se lève rouge. Plus de 200 ans plus tard, les cernes des arbres ont donné la réponse.
